name: BqLog
workload: 1-10 threads each writing 2,000,000 log entries with 4 parameters; total time cost in ms, versus spdlog async, glog, fmtlog, quill, Log4j2.
claimed_speedup: Compressed mode 6-65x faster than spdlog (async) and 47-252x faster than glog; e.g. 4 params, 4 threads: BqLog Compress 210 ms vs spdlog async 5737 ms vs glog 21387 ms; 10 threads: 507 ms vs 32939 ms vs 127550 ms
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 14.51, Release x64 (no extra flags stated)
stars_or_usage: Tencent; used in Honor of Kings
tradeoffs: Compressed binary log format needs BqLog tooling to decode; multi-language (Java, C#, Python, Go, TS) with Unity and Unreal support; 'Text' mode is slower than Compress mode.
caveats: Windows/MSVC only in the headline run; vendor-run benchmark (the code is public in the benchmark_2.5.0 tag); the README headline compares the compressed binary mode, not text output; the benchmark output mode of each competitor may differ.
found_via: WebSearch 'logger benchmark comparison spdlog quill fmtlog binlog'; then README and docs/BENCHMARK.md

name: Quill
workload: Hot-path logging latency (single and multi-thread; numbers, large strings, complex types) and backend throughput, versus spdlog, fmtlog, Boost.Log and others.
claimed_speedup: 1 thread logging numbers: 6 ns (90th percentile) vs spdlog 296 ns, Boost.Log 3259 ns; large strings multi-thread 14 ns vs spdlog 588 ns; throughput 6.44 M msg/s vs spdlog 2.57 M msg/s, Boost.Log 0.33 M msg/s
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2, Release, -march=x86-64-v3, RHEL 9.4 with benchmark-specific kernel tuning
tradeoffs: Formatting and I/O happen on a backend thread; per-thread SPSC queues use memory; C++17.
caveats: Benchmark code lives in the author's own logger_benchmarks repo (https://github.com/odygrd/logger_benchmarks), first-party; glog not in the README table.
found_via: WebSearch 'low latency C++ logging library faster than spdlog benchmark github'

name: fmtlog
workload: Per-call latency and throughput logging a static string and two integers, versus NanoLog and spdlog.
claimed_speedup: Static string: 6.4 ns vs spdlog 156.4 ns; two integers: 6.4 ns vs spdlog 257.2 ns (throughput 4.87 M/s vs 3.89 M/s)
tradeoffs: Depends on fmtlib; background thread polls; log order maintained across threads.
caveats: Compiler and flags are not stated on the README page opened (bench/bench.cc is public, so tier set to C for missing compiler and flags); first-party; the independent cc_log_benchmark also ranks it among the fastest.
found_via: WebSearch 'asynchronous logger nanosecond latency hot path benchmark spdlog glog comparison github'

name: NanoLog (Stanford PlatformLab)
baseline: spdlog v1.1.0, glog v0.3.5, Log4j2 v2.8, Boost 1.55
workload: Runtime log-call latency (50th/99.9th percentile) and max throughput for six message types, with a compile-time log preprocessor and binary runtime log.
claimed_speedup: Median ~7-8 ns vs spdlog 214-1776 ns and glog 1198-2569 ns; staticString 7/37 ns vs spdlog 214/2546 ns, glog 1198/5968 ns; over 80 million logs/s
tradeoffs: Needs a compile-time preprocessor step and a decompressor to read logs; C++17 and POSIX AIO; format strings must be literals.
caveats: Peer reviewed in the USENIX ATC 2018 paper (not opened, blocked); README page gives no hardware or flags; competitor versions are old (spdlog 1.1.0, 2018).
found_via: WebSearch 'asynchronous logger nanosecond latency hot path ...'; README performance section

name: NanoLog (Iyengar111)
workload: Microsecond-percentile log-call latency with 1-5 threads versus spdlog, g3log and reckless.
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: NanoLog guaranteed 50th=0 us, 99th=4 us, worst=68 us vs spdlog 3/5/129 us and g3log 5/10/186 us; non-guaranteed logger ~131-383 ns average
tradeoffs: Non-guaranteed mode drops messages when the ring buffer is full; header and cpp pair; C++11.
caveats: No LICENSE file found (404 on raw LICENSE); very old toolchain and hardware; reckless has a lower 99th percentile in some rows; first-party; microsecond resolution only.
found_via: WebSearch 'low latency C++ logging library faster than spdlog benchmark github'

name: lockfreelog
workload: Messages per second through a header-only SPSC ring-buffer logger, versus spdlog async, fmt, iostream and printf.
claimed_speedup: ~28M msgs/s vs spdlog async ~5M msgs/s (5.3x faster) and printf ~12M (2.3x) on Apple M3; ~50M msgs/s on Xeon Gold 6348
hardware: Apple M3; Intel Xeon Gold 6348 (Ice Lake)
tradeoffs: C++20 header-only; SPSC only per ring; no heap allocation; a slot-full policy decides blocking or dropping (not checked).
caveats: No license in the repo; 3 commits; author-run; the Xeon figure has no spdlog ratio on the page; whether spdlog was configured to an equivalent output was not verified (bench/benchmark.cpp unopened).
found_via: WebSearch 'C logging library lock-free ring buffer faster than glog spdlog benchmark github'

name: low-latency-log
workload: Hot-path latency percentiles and backend throughput, 2M messages per thread, 1 and 4 threads.
claimed_speedup: M3 Max: 4.563 M msgs/s vs C++ quill 2.88, spdlog-rs 2.605, fast_log 1.741, ftlog 1.688 (median hot-path 58 ns vs spdlog-rs 252 ns, but quill 22 ns)
hardware: MacBook Pro M3 Max 48GB; Xeon Gold 6231C
tradeoffs: Part of the code derives from logflume under a separate license; Rust only.
caveats: Does not beat spdlog or glog directly (compared to spdlog-rs and C++ quill); quill has lower median hot-path latency in the same file; first-party.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust logging library faster than log crate ...'

name: fastrace
workload: Cost of creating and finishing traces with 1 to 1000 spans, on four architectures, versus tokio-tracing and rustracing.
claimed_speedup: tokio-tracing 124x slower on Intel Broadwell (33x Skylake, 36x AMD Zen, 29x Graviton2); 19x slower at 1 span, 151x at 1000 spans; fastrace baseline 3.4 us
hardware: Intel Broadwell, Intel Skylake, AMD Zen, AWS Graviton2
tradeoffs: Library-level tracing with tail-sampling; no 'level' concept; compatible with OpenTelemetry export via fastrace-opentelemetry; MSRV 1.91.
caveats: Baseline is tokio-tracing, not the OpenTelemetry SDK; result tables are in README and benches/results (not opened); compiler flags not stated; successor of minitrace.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust logging tracing crate faster than tracing-subscriber benchmark nanosecond github'

name: phuslu/log
workload: Go structured JSON logging ns/op and allocations: simple message and with caller information.
claimed_speedup: Simple: 214.2 ns/op vs zap 823.7, zerolog 337.6, slog 1274; with caller: 546.1 vs zap 2249, zerolog 1375, slog 2155; 50-100% faster as slog.JSONHandler replacement
tradeoffs: Zero allocation in common paths; Go only; zerolog-inspired API.
caveats: Baselines are Go loggers, not spdlog, glog or OpenTelemetry; Go version and flags not stated; first-party.
found_via: WebSearch 'Go zero allocation structured logger benchmark faster than zap zerolog github'
